pedagogy.summary: By ages 11-13 children can grasp that we detect planets around other stars indirectly, by watching the STAR rather than seeing the planet. Teach the two workhorse methods as detective clues: (1) the TRANSIT method — when a planet crosses in front of its star, the star's light dips by a tiny, repeating amount; the size of the dip encodes the planet's size and the spacing between dips encodes the orbital period; (2) RADIAL VELOCITY — a planet's gravity tugs the star into a small wobble, alternately squeezing (bluer) and stretching (redder) the star's light. Layer on the idea of the HABITABLE ZONE (the orbital band where liquid water is possible) and BIOSIGNATURES (atmospheric gases, e.g. oxygen and methane co-existing, that might hint at life). The core conceptual move is indirect inference: reasoning from a shadow-like signal back to an unseen cause.
bestPractices: Frame it as forensic reasoning: you never see the planet, you read its fingerprints on the star's light — build the habit of inferring an unseen cause from a measured signal
Start with the transit light-curve as a story: flat line (star alone), a dip (planet crossing), flat again — then vary planet size and orbit to show which feature of the graph changes
Make the two methods complementary, not competing: transit gives size, radial velocity gives mass; together they give density and hence rough composition (rocky vs gas)
Use real discovery data (Kepler/TESS light curves; 51 Pegasi b as the first around a Sun-like star) so the signal feels real, not idealised
Address scale honestly: dips are often <1% of the star's brightness — the achievement is measuring something so faint so precisely, which is why space telescopes help
Introduce habitable zone as 'not too hot, not too cold for liquid water' but stress it is a necessary-not-sufficient hint, avoiding 'habitable = inhabited'
keyRepresentations: Transit light-curve graph (brightness vs time) with a periodic dip — the canonical exoplanet representation
Side-by-side star+planet orbit view coupled to the light curve so the dip lines up with the moment of crossing
Doppler wobble diagram: star tracing a small circle, its spectrum shifting blue then red
Habitable-zone band diagram: a star with a coloured 'Goldilocks' ring at the right distance
Transmission-spectrum 'barcode' showing dark lines where an atmosphere's gases absorb light
commonMisconceptions: 'We take photos of the planets' — almost all exoplanets are found indirectly; direct images are rare and show dots, not worlds
'A dip in brightness means the star is dimming/dying' — it is a temporary, repeating eclipse by an orbiting planet, not a change in the star
'In the habitable zone = has life / has water' — the zone only means liquid water is possible given the right atmosphere; it is a candidacy, not a confirmation
'Radial velocity means the star is really moving toward us across space' — it is a tiny back-and-forth wobble about the system's centre of mass, read from spectral shifts
'Bigger dip = closer planet' — dip DEPTH tracks planet SIZE relative to the star; orbital distance shows up in the PERIOD (spacing of dips), not the depth
'One gas proves life' — biosignatures rely on combinations out of chemical equilibrium (e.g. oxygen plus methane together), and even then are debated

learn.summary: Teach 11-13s how astronomers detect planets around other stars indirectly, by reading effects on the STAR rather than seeing the planet. The core conceptual move is inferring an unseen cause from a measured signal. Centre the work on two methods: (1) the TRANSIT method — a planet crossing in front of its star makes starlight dip by a tiny, repeating amount, where dip DEPTH encodes planet size (relative to the star) and dip SPACING encodes orbital period; (2) RADIAL VELOCITY — a planet's gravity tugs the star into a small wobble about the system's centre of mass, shifting its light bluer (approaching) then redder (receding). Layer on the habitable zone (orbital band where liquid water could exist) and biosignatures (atmospheric gas combinations out of equilibrium, e.g. oxygen with methane, that might hint at life). Stress necessary-not-sufficient reasoning: habitable zone is candidacy not confirmation, and one gas is not proof of life.

activities.title: Build the planet, watch its light-curve fingerprint
feedback: If a learner expects a bigger planet to space the dips out, point them back to the controls: size only deepens the dip; it is the orbit control that changes spacing — these are two separate planet properties read from two separate graph features

If a learner says 'bigger dip = closer planet', have them hold size fixed and change only the orbit: the depth stays the same while the spacing changes, showing distance lives in the period not the depth

If a learner reads the dip as the star fading or dying, clarify that in this model it is a temporary, repeating eclipse by the orbiting planet, not a change in the star's own output; the dip recurs on a regular schedule because the planet comes round again on each orbit. A star that was really fading for good would not brighten back up after each dip. (Some real stars do change brightness in regular cycles, so astronomers also check the dip's shape and use other methods.)
In detective mode, if a reconstruction is off, ask which feature is wrong — depth (adjust size) or spacing (adjust period) — rather than adjusting both at once
activities.rationale: The concept is a relationship between a hidden cause (orbiting planet) and a measured signal (light curve / spectral wobble). A model that RECOMPUTES the graph live as the learner changes the planet lets them discover for themselves that depth tracks size and spacing tracks period; detective mode forces the inference from signal back to cause, which is the real objective. The size↔depth and period↔spacing couplings are independent comparisons and must be varied one at a time.
sourceClaims: Transit method: planets crossing in front of their star cause tiny repeating dips in starlight; orbital size is derived from the period plus the star's mass; used by Kepler and TESS

Radial velocity: a star's light wavelengths are alternately squeezed and stretched as the star moves slightly closer then farther due to an orbiting planet's gravitational tug; 51 Pegasi b was the first found around a Sun-like star this way
learnerActions: Drag a small planet onto an orbit around a star; below, a brightness-vs-time line traces across the screen in real time as the planet crosses in front of the star — flat line (star alone), a dip (planet crossing), flat again
Grab a SIZE control and watch the dip get DEEPER as the planet grows; grab an ORBIT RADIUS / PERIOD control and watch the SPACING between dips stretch out and transits grow rarer
State in your own words which graph feature encodes planet size and which encodes orbital period
Enter 'detective mode', which hides the planet and gives you only a wiggly light curve: set size and period to reconstruct the planet that must have produced it

Flip a RADIAL-VELOCITY toggle to see the same planet betrayed a second way — the star wobbling about the system's centre of mass, its spectrum shifting blue (approaching) then red (receding), plotted on a second graph
activities.intendedInsight: We never see the planet; we read its fingerprints on the star's light. Dip DEPTH tracks planet SIZE relative to the star, while orbital distance shows up in the PERIOD (spacing of dips), not the depth. Two independent signals (transit and wobble) can reveal the same unseen world.

activities.title: Name the parts of a light curve and the Goldilocks band
feedback: If a learner reads the habitable zone as 'this planet has water/life', restate it as where liquid water COULD exist given the right atmosphere — a candidacy, not a confirmation
If a learner reads the whole spectrum as one signal, point to individual dark lines and note each marks a specific gas absorbing light
activities.rationale: A static annotated diagram with tap-to-reveal facts is a clean way to name parts and fix vocabulary. It is a scaffold: on its own it names the labels without letting the learner feel the size↔depth / period↔spacing coupling, so it works best alongside or after the interactive model.
learnerActions: Study a labelled light curve (flat–dip–flat) and identify the moment of crossing, the depth of the dip, and the gap between dips
Reveal that the dip corresponds to the planet crossing (a deeper dip means a bigger planet compared with its star) and the gap between dips corresponds to the orbit time (period)
Examine a habitable-zone band diagram — a star with a coloured 'Goldilocks' ring at the right distance — and state the definition: 'not too hot, not too cold for liquid water'
Inspect a transmission-spectrum 'barcode' showing dark lines where an atmosphere's gases absorb light, and read off which gases a spectrum reveals
activities.intendedInsight: Lock the vocabulary: dip depth, dip spacing/period, habitable zone, transmission spectrum. Naming the parts supports, but does not replace, reasoning about why depth and spacing encode different things.

activities.title: Read-the-graph consolidation challenges
feedback: If a learner picks the wrong light-curve match, ask them to compare depths first (size) and then spacings (period) separately
If a learner says a single gas proves life, note that biosignatures rely on COMBINATIONS out of chemical equilibrium (oxygen plus methane together), and even then are debated
activities.rationale: Recognition and matching tasks are good for consolidating the read-the-graph skill after the interactive model; as a first encounter they test recall without building the causal intuition, so they are placed as follow-up rather than introduction. Recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the signal-to-cause inference.
learnerActions: Match a given light curve to the planet that produced it, choosing from several candidates
Identify which graph feature encodes size and which encodes period
Set the dip depth for a Jupiter-sized versus an Earth-sized planet orbiting the same Sun-like star

Match each tool to what it measures: transit → size, radial velocity → mass (on its own only a lower limit, but a true mass when the planet also transits); and explain that together they give density and hence rough composition (rocky vs gas)
Answer a question on the oxygen+methane biosignature logic: why two out-of-equilibrium gases together are a stronger hint than either alone
activities.intendedInsight: Transit gives size, radial velocity gives mass, and the two together give density and hence a rough idea of composition (rocky vs gas). Consolidating the read-the-graph skill confirms the learner can apply the depth/period distinction rather than merely recognise it.

activities.title: In role: hunting a real candidate signal
feedback: If a learner accepts a single dip as proof, ask what else could dim a star once; stress that a regular repetition each orbit is needed, but even a repeating dip can have other causes (such as a pair of stars eclipsing each other), so astronomers also check it with other evidence, such as a radial-velocity wobble, before confirming a planet
If a learner treats the wobble as the star genuinely travelling across space toward us, clarify it is a tiny back-and-forth wobble about the system's centre of mass, read from spectral shifts

If a learner asks why we don't just photograph the planet directly, note exoplanets are almost always far too faint and too close to their dazzling star to image directly; the rare direct images show only dots, not worlds — which is why we read the star's light instead
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue with real discovery data (51 Peg b, Kepler/TESS) can convey the thrill and the reasoning and make the signal feel real rather than idealised. Dialogue motivates and narrates the inference but does not itself show the light curve recompute, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive model.
sourceClaims: Radial velocity: a star's light wavelengths are alternately squeezed and stretched as the star moves slightly closer then farther due to an orbiting planet's gravitational tug; 51 Pegasi b was the first found around a Sun-like star this way
Transit method: planets crossing in front of their star cause tiny repeating dips in starlight; orbital size is derived from the period plus the star's mass; used by Kepler and TESS
learnerActions: Take on the role of an exoplanet hunter talking with a mission scientist who walks you through a real candidate signal (e.g. a Kepler/TESS light curve, or the 51 Pegasi b wobble)
Explain what you would measure next to confirm the signal really is a planet, and why the pattern needs to REPEAT periodically
Discuss why dips are often less than 1% of the star's brightness, and why measuring something so faint so precisely is the real achievement (and why space telescopes help)
activities.intendedInsight: Confirmation needs a repeating, periodic signal, because a single one-off dim is not enough. Even a repeating signal must be checked against other causes, often with a second method such as radial velocity. Framing detection as forensic reasoning builds the habit of inferring an unseen cause from a measured signal using real discovery data.

constraints: Avoid 'habitable = inhabited': the habitable zone means liquid water is possible given the right atmosphere; it is a necessary-not-sufficient candidacy, not a confirmation of water or life
Avoid 'one gas proves life': biosignatures rely on combinations out of chemical equilibrium (oxygen plus methane together), and even these are debated
A static labelled diagram fixes vocabulary but cannot let the learner feel the size↔depth and period↔spacing couplings; treat it as a scaffold used with or after the interactive model
Recognition/matching tasks consolidate the read-the-graph skill but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the signal-to-cause inference
Keep size and period comparisons separate: changing size deepens the dip; changing orbit changes the spacing of dips — do not let a learner conclude depth tracks distance
A dip is a temporary, repeating eclipse by an orbiting planet, not the star dimming or dying; the star's own brightness is unchanged, and the dip repeats because the planet returns each orbit

Treat the orbit as a 1D brightness signal over time, not spatial 3D structure; a 3D rendering of the orbit is not needed to teach the inference, though this reflects the task's nature, not a universal claim about 3D
Address scale honestly: dips are often <1% of the star's brightness, and the precision of measuring so faint a signal is itself the achievement
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's fourth claim (habitable zone definition and oxygen+methane biosignatures) is marked verified:false in the row ('General astrobiology consensus, not confirmed against a single fetched page this session'); treat the habitable-zone and biosignature content as reflecting general consensus rather than a verified fetched source. It was kept out of sourceClaims arrays.

The original row framed radial velocity as giving MASS and transit as giving SIZE, combining to density/composition; the fetched sources explicitly support transit→period/orbit and the RV Doppler wobble, but the depth↔size and density/composition synthesis are standard inferences stated in pedagogy rather than directly quoted in sources[].claim — kept as teaching content, flagged here.
Radial velocity strictly yields a minimum mass (m sin i); presenting it as 'mass' is an age-appropriate simplification but is firmer than the source wording.

The row's non-preferred '3D adds nothing' phrasing was softened to a scoped observation that detection is a 1D time signal; the claim that 3D is universally useless is not established by catalog ratings.

SourceClaims were attached only to activities 1 and 4, which teach the transit and radial-velocity mechanisms the claims establish; activities 2 and 3 are set to [] because their rationales are purely about vocabulary scaffolding and recall consolidation.
Agent adjusted activity 1 feedback so repetition of the dip is attributed to the planet's periodic orbit rather than to the star's brightness being unchanged.

probeDeeper: If a star dims briefly just once and never again, would you call that a planet — and why does the pattern need to repeat?
Why is finding oxygen AND methane together more exciting than finding either one alone?
Does being in the habitable zone guarantee a planet has water and life, or just make it possible?
Why can't we simply point a telescope at the star and photograph its planets?
assess.correctAnswer: They detect the planet INDIRECTLY, from its effect on the star, not by photographing it. In the transit method, the planet crossing in front of its star causes a tiny, regular DIP in the star's brightness each orbit; in the radial-velocity method, the planet's gravity makes the star WOBBLE slightly, shifting its light toward red then blue (Doppler). The repeating, periodic pattern is what confirms it's a planet. As for oxygen: on its own it doesn't prove life, because some non-living processes make it too. Far more telling is finding gases TOGETHER that shouldn't coexist unless something keeps replenishing them — oxygen AND methane at once — which would strongly hint at active life. And a planet must be in the habitable zone (where liquid water could exist) to be a promising place to look.

errorPatterns.pattern: we find exoplanets by taking direct photos of them, like photographing Jupiter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain exoplanets are almost always inferred from the star's dimming or wobble — they're far too faint and too close to their dazzling star to photograph directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: Astronomers know the planet is there because they photographed it directly through a powerful telescope.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child assumes a direct image of the planet was taken

errorPatterns.pattern: finding oxygen (or any single gas) proves there is life
errorPatterns.nextMove: Non-living processes can produce oxygen; the strong hint is gases that shouldn't coexist — like oxygen and methane together — needing constant replenishment by something active.
errorPatterns.distractor: Detecting oxygen in the planet's air proves there must be life there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats one biosignature as proof of life

errorPatterns.pattern: a planet in the habitable zone definitely has life or liquid water
errorPatterns.nextMove: The habitable zone is only where liquid water COULD exist given the right conditions — a promising place to look, not a guarantee of water or life.
errorPatterns.distractor: If a planet is in the habitable zone, it must have life on it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child equates 'in the habitable zone' with 'inhabited'

responseLevels.gap: Thinks we photograph exoplanets directly and/or that one gas proves life.
responseLevels.full: Explains indirect detection (transit dip and/or Doppler wobble confirmed by periodic repetition), the habitable zone as where water could exist, and why out-of-equilibrium co-present gases (oxygen + methane) are a far stronger life hint than any single gas.
responseLevels.partial: Explains one detection method OR that biosignatures matter, but misses the role of periodic repetition or why co-present gases are the key signal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Astronomers announce they've found a planet orbiting a star hundreds of light-years away — but they never actually took a picture of the planet itself. How can they know it's there? And if they later detect oxygen in its air, does that prove there's life? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who assumes we photograph exoplanets directly cannot explain the detection. A child who understands indirect inference describes the transit dip or Doppler wobble and the role of periodic repetition. The biosignature half separates 'oxygen = life' from the subtler 'co-present out-of-equilibrium gases hint at life'. The 'why' tier tests both inferential moves.
